What is the storehouse consciousness?.label: storehouse consciousness
What is the storehouse consciousness?.answer_html_plain: According to Sthiramati on the Triṃśikā, the storehouse consciousness is ālayavijñāna (“storehouse/repository consciousness”): it is so called because ālaya means sthāna (“place/support”), the place of the seeds of all defiled dharmas, and because all dharmas are “lodged/bound” in it as effects while it is lodged/bound in them as cause [trimsika 2]. It is also the sarvabījaṃ vijñānam (“all-seeded consciousness”), meaning ālayavijñāna insofar as it carries the powers/seeds capable of producing all dharmas [trimsika 18]. Textual support: - Sthiramati glosses ālaya as sthāna (“place/support”): “It is ālaya because it is the place of the seeds of all defiled dharmas; ālaya and sthāna are synonyms” [trimsika 2]. - He further explains the name by saying that all dharmas are bound in it as effects, and it is bound in all dharmas as cause [trimsika 2]. - He identifies “all-seeded consciousness” with ālayavijñāna because it is accompanied by the power to produce all dharmas [trimsika 18]. - This ālayavijñāna is a kind of vijñānapariṇāma (“transformation of consciousness”), where pariṇāma means a dependently arisen transformation or “becoming otherwise” [trimsika 1]. - It is distinct from manas (“mind”), since Sthiramati says the consciousness named manas relies on ālayavijñāna and has it as its object, thereby distinguishing manas from ālayavijñāna [trimsika 5].

What does representation-only (vijñapti-.label: representation-only
What does representation-only (vijñapti-.answer_html_plain: Directly: In Sthiramati’s Triṃśikā commentary, vijñapti-mātra (“representation-only”) means that what is imagined as an object-domain is absent, so “all this” is only representation; ultimately it is the citta-dharmatā (“nature/reality of mind”) marked by advaya (“non-duality”). [trimsika 17] [trimsika 26] Textual support: - Sthiramati explains “all this is representation-only” by saying that whatever object is imagined by vikalpa (“constructive imagination”)—such as world, self, aggregates, sense-bases, form, sound, etc.—“does not exist”; therefore, because of viṣayābhāva (“absence of an object-domain”), everything is vijñaptimātraka (“representation-only”). [trimsika 17] - This is not a nihilistic denial: Sthiramati frames the verse as avoiding the extreme of denial after rejecting superimposition. [trimsika 17] - At the level of realization, Sthiramati glosses vijñaptimātratva (“representation-only-ness”) as the dharmatā of mind designated “representation-only,” and as having advaya-lakṣaṇa (“non-duality as its mark”). [trimsika 26] - Cognition is established in representation-only when it no longer apprehends an ālambana (“object-support”), because the appearance of something graspable is absent. [trimsika 28] - Failure to abide in that mere representation persists so long as the apprehension of consciousness has not been abandoned. [trimsika 27]

What does the Gita say about acting with.label: karma without attachment
What does the Gita say about acting with.answer_html_plain: The Gītā, as explained by Śaṅkara, teaches that one should act without desire for the karma-phala (“fruit/result of action”), but should not become attached to akarmaṇi (“non-performance”): even if one does not seek the fruit, one must not think, “what is the use of painful action?” and abandon action out of fondness for inaction [gita 2.47]. Śaṅkara also explains saṅgaṃ tyaktvā (“having abandoned attachment”) in Gītā 2.48 as giving up even subtle attachment such as the thought “īśvaro me tuṣyatu” (“may Īśvara be pleased with me”) [gita 2.48]. So, acting without attachment to results means: do the action, do not cling to its fruit, and do not use non-attachment as a reason to avoid action [gita 2.47]; relinquish attachment even to religiously framed expectations from the action [gita 2.48].

Why does Krishna tell Arjuna not to grie.label: why not grieve
Why does Krishna tell Arjuna not to grie.answer_html_plain: Kṛṣṇa tells Arjuna not to grieve because the wise, “knowers of the Self,” do not grieve either for the dead or the living; those Arjuna mourns are aśocyāḥ (“not to be grieved for”). [gita 2.11] He also grounds this in the continuity of persons beyond bodily destruction, saying that he, Arjuna, and the kings were not nonexistent before and will not be nonexistent afterward. [gita 2.12] Further, death and rebirth are aparihārya (“inevitable”): for one born, death is certain, and for one dead, birth is certain, so Arjuna “should not grieve” over such an unavoidable matter. [gita 2.27] Śaṅkara adds that Arjuna ought not grieve on the false thought, “I am their slayer; by me these are slain.” [gita 2.25] Even if one were to suppose birth and death belong to the self, Śaṅkara says grief is still unwarranted because destruction of what is born and birth of what is destroyed are inevitable. [gita 2.26] Finally, the dehī (“embodied one”) is described as always avadhyaḥ (“not to be killed”) in the body of every being; therefore Arjuna ought not grieve for any beings. [gita 2.30]

Who is the person of steady wisdom (sthi.label: steady wisdom
Who is the person of steady wisdom (sthi.answer_html_plain: Direct answer: According to Śaṅkara on the Gītā, the sthita-prajña (“one whose prajñā, wisdom/cognition, is established”) is a person—not an abstract “steady wisdom”—whose established wisdom is the cognition “I am the supreme Brahman,” and who is a vidvān (“wise person”) whose wisdom is born from ātman-anātman-viveka (“discrimination of Self and non-Self”). [gita 2.54] [gita 2.55] Textual support: - Gītā 2.55 says that when one abandons all kāmān (“desires”) lodged in the mind and is content in the ātman (“Self”) alone, by the Self itself, he is called sthita-prajña. [gita 2.55] - Śaṅkara glosses this person as a saṃnyāsī (“renunciant”) who has abandoned desire for sons, wealth, and worlds, and who delights and sports in the Self. [gita 2.55] - Śaṅkara also describes this person as one whose discrimination-born wisdom is established and who is free from joy and sorrow. [gita 2.57]

What happens to the soul at death, accor.label: the soul at death
What happens to the soul at death, accor.answer_html_plain: According to the provided Gītā passages as read by Śaṅkara, at death beings pass out of manifestation: they are avyakta (“unmanifest,” i.e. unseen/not apprehended) after maraṇa/nidhana (“death”). Śaṅkara explains that bhūtāni (“beings”) are unmanifest before birth, manifest between birth and death, and after death “attain only unmanifestness” [gita 2.28]. If one hypothetically treats ātman (“self/soul”) as subject to birth and death, Śaṅkara says grief is still unwarranted, because destruction for what is born and birth for what has been destroyed are inevitable [gita 2.26]. The passages provided do not give the fuller Gītā teaching on the soul’s immortality or its post-mortem journey beyond this unmanifest/manifest framing.

How does Vyasa define yoga?.label: definition of yoga
How does Vyasa define yoga?.answer_html_plain: Vyāsa defines yoga (“yoga”) technically as samādhi (“concentration/absorption”): “yogaḥ samādhiḥ”—“Yoga is samādhi” [yogasutra 1.1, justification]. He further explains the sūtra-definition as “cittavṛttinirodha” (“restraint of the fluctuations of citta/mind-stuff”), and says this yoga is twofold: saṃprajñāta (“with distinct cognition”) and asaṃprajñāta (“without distinct cognition”) [yogasutra 1.2, justification]. Textual support: Vyāsa says distracted samādhi is not yoga; rather, saṃprajñāta yoga is the one-pointed samādhi that illumines a real object, weakens kleśa (“afflictions”), loosens karmic bonds, and turns toward nirodha (“restraint/cessation”) [yogasutra 1.1, justification]. When all vṛtti (“mental fluctuations”) cease, it is asaṃprajñāta samādhi [yogasutra 1.1, justification]. Since the sūtra does not say “all,” Vyāsa explicitly includes saṃprajñāta also under yoga, not only total objectless cessation [yogasutra 1.2, justification].

What is the role of practice and dispass.label: practice and dispassion
What is the role of practice and dispass.answer_html_plain: According to Vyāsa on the Yogasūtra, abhyāsa (“practice”) and vairāgya (“dispassion”) are the two jointly operative means for yoga’s cittavṛttinirodha (“cessation of mental fluctuations”): dispassion blocks the mind’s current toward objects, while practice opens the current toward discriminative seeing.[yogasutra 1.12] Textual support: - Vyāsa says the citta (“consciousness/mind”) is like a river flowing in two directions: toward kaivalya (“isolation/liberation”) through viveka (“discrimination”), or toward saṃsāra through non-discrimination.[yogasutra 1.12] - Vairāgya makes the viṣaya-srotas (“stream toward objects”) barren, and vivekadarśanābhyāsa (“practice of discriminative seeing”) opens the viveka-srotas (“stream of discrimination”).[yogasutra 1.12] - Therefore, Vyāsa explicitly states that cessation of mental fluctuations is dependent on both practice and dispassion, not on either alone.[yogasutra 1.12] - In Vyāsa’s account of the path to asaṃprajñāta samādhi (“samādhi without cognitive content”), faith leads to energy, energy to recollection, recollection to concentration, concentration to discriminating insight, and from practice of that insight plus dispassion toward each object, asaṃprajñāta samādhi arises.[yogasutra 1.20] - Vyāsa defines a grade of dispassion as non-engagement toward objects, arising from seeing their defects through discriminative discernment, and as empty of both appropriation and rejection.[yogasutra 1.15]

How can the mind be made calm and clear?.label: calming the mind
How can the mind be made calm and clear?.answer_html_plain: Directly: the passages say the mind becomes calm and clear through cultivation/training that removes restlessness and heaviness, makes a suitable object directly present, and produces serenity, one-pointedness, and steadiness; the exact practice meant by “cultivates in this way” in Yogasūtra 1.33 is not included in the supplied passage. [yogasutra 1.33] [yogasutra 1.35] - Vyāsa on Yogasūtra 1.33 says that for one who “cultivates in this way,” citta (“mind”) becomes prasanna (“clear/serene”); once clear, it becomes ekāgra (“one-pointed”) and reaches sthitipada (“a state of steadiness”). [yogasutra 1.33] - Vyāsa on Yogasūtra 1.35 says cittaparikarma (“purification/training of the mind”) is taught so that a particular object is made direct, doubt is dispelled, and samādhi-prajñā (“insight born of samādhi”) is opened; then faith, energy, memory, and samādhi arise unobstructed. [yogasutra 1.35] - Sthiramati says auddhatya (“restlessness/non-tranquillity”) is the mind’s lack of calm and obstructs śamatha (“calm”); it arises from attachment-favorable recollection of former laughter, talk, play, and the like. [trimsika 13] - Sthiramati also says praśrabdhi (“pliancy/workability”) counters dauṣṭhulya (“heaviness/unworkability”) and lets the correctly attentive mind proceed unobstructed toward its object with joy and lightness. [trimsika 11]

What does 'all this is pervaded by the L.label: īśāvāsyam
What does 'all this is pervaded by the L.answer_html_plain: For Śaṅkara on Īśa 1, “all this is pervaded by the Lord” means: all this world is to be “covered/enveloped” by the Lord, understood as one’s own supreme Self, the inward Self of all, in the realization “I alone am all this.” [isa 1, justification] Textually, īśā (“by the Lord”) is glossed as īśena / ātmanā (“by the Lord / by the Self”), and the Lord is identified as parameśvaraḥ paramātmā sarvasya (“the Supreme Lord, the supreme Self of all”). [isa 1, justification] vāsyam (“to be covered/enveloped”) is not taken by Śaṅkara as “to be inhabited” or “to be used,” but as ācchādanīyam (“to be covered”). [isa 1, justification] “All this” refers to the moving-and-unmoving world, which is to be covered by one’s own paramātman (“supreme Self”), as sandalwood’s true fragrance covers an adventitious bad odor. [isa 1, justification]

Can one wish to live a hundred years per.label: a hundred years of works
Can one wish to live a hundred years per.answer_html_plain: Yes—but in Śaṅkara’s reading of Īśā 2, the Upaniṣad is not independently enjoining a desire for longevity; it is saying that one who wishes to live should live while performing prescribed ritual works. [isa 2, justification] Here jijīviṣet (“should wish/seek to live”) with śataṃ samāḥ (“a hundred years”) can be translated “one should seek to live a hundred years,” but Śaṅkara treats the wish for long life as prāptānuvāda (“restatement of an already natural fact”), while the real injunction is kurvan eva karmāṇi (“only doing works”). [isa 2, justification] Those karmāṇi (“works”) are specifically śāstra-vihitāni karmāṇi (“scripture-enjoined works”), such as Agnihotra and the like, not ordinary secular activity. [isa 2, justification] Thus the verse says: “Only doing here the ritual works, one should seek to live a hundred years”; for such a person, “there is no other way” by which action does not cling. [isa 2, translation]
